questions.question: Discuss the structural features of rural society and analyse how they sustain / traditional community life
questions.solution_html:
• community life.
  • Rural society refers to communities located in villages where life is closely connected with
  • nature, agriculture, and traditional social systems. These societies have unique structural
  • features that strongly influence community life.
  • Proximity and Stability:Traditional rural life is built on "proximity, continuity and stability,"
  • which act as a crucible for community ties.
  • Multiplex Relationships:Residents experience "linked multiple relationships" (multiplexity)
  • where the same people are encountered in various roles (e.g., neighbor, workmate, fellow
  • worshiper).
  • Mechanical Solidarity:Rural villages often display "mechanical solidarity," where similarity
  • in backgrounds and "common ways of thinking and feeling" create a dense social web.
  • Organic Connection to Place: The village is often viewed as an "organic" context
  • slow-growing and in harmony with its agricultural environment, providing a common
  • purpose.
  • Rural social structure plays a crucial role in maintaining traditional community life, though
  • gradual change is necessary to balance tradition with development.
questions.final_answer: gradual change is necessary to balance tradition with development
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Discuss the importance of training in Community Psychology. / What competencies are required for effective community practice?
questions.solution_html:
• required for effective community practice?
  • Community psychology focuses on promoting well-being through social change and
  • community-based interventions. Proper training is essential for effective practice.
  • Importance of Training
  • Professionalization: community work has shifted from marginal, voluntary activity to a
  • "professionalized" field and a "significant industry".
  • Growing Field of Employment:There is an expanding demand for community workers
  • facilitators, and experts to manage "regeneration, participation and intervention" .
  • Technical Requirements:Modern community practice requires "monitoring and
  • evaluation" as key components of project work to meet the performance criteria and
  • targets set by funding bodies.
  • Required Competencies
  • Analytical Skills:Practitioners must be able to conduct "local needs assessments
  • community audits and village appraisals" and construct "community profiles".
  • Research Adaptation: Effective practice involves adapting social scientific techniques
  • (quantitative and qualitative) so they can be understood and utilized by "ordinary people"
  • within the community.
  • Facilitation and Leadership:Professionals act as "consultants, facilitators, and
  • intermediaries" who lead divided communities toward cooperation and conflict resolution.
  • Capacity-Building:A core competency is the ability to enable "capacity-building
  • measures" that empower community members to take ownership of local processes and
  • tackle their own priorities.
  • Training equips community psychologists with essential competencies to bring meaningful
  • and sustainable social change.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Examine the limitations of Western measures of control when applied to non - / Western collectivistic communities
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the limitations of Western measures of control when applied to non-Western
  • collectivistic communities.
  • Western psychological concepts are largely based on individualism, which may not suit
  • collectivistic societies like India.
  • Individualism vs. Responsibilities: Western models often emphasize individual "rights,"
  • whereas collectivistic communities may prioritize "responsibilities" and the "moral voice" of
  • the group to enforce behavior.
  • Mislabeling Disorganization: Outside observers often view dense, complex urban or poor
  • areas as "disorganized," when they actually possess a well-defined internal social order
  • (e.g., "ordered segmentation") invisible to outsiders.
  • Informal vs. Formal Controls: Western measures often rely on bureaucratic agencies
  • while collectivistic communities use informal sanctions like "gentle chastisement," gossip, or
  • even exclusion to maintain order.
  • Western models need cultural adaptation to be effective in non-Western collectivistic
  • societies
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Compare information dissemination and community education. / Highlight their similarities and differences.
questions.solution_html:
• Compare information dissemination and community education. Highlight their similarities
  • and differences.
  • Both information dissemination and community education are methods used to create
  • awareness and promote social development.
  • Information Dissemination
  • Abstract Systems: In modern, "disembedded" social relations, people rely on "abstract
  • systems of information" rather than personal knowledge .
  • Top-Down Control: It is often a "top-down" tool used by "urban managers" or the state to
  • frame the parameters of community life or to "label" specific areas and groups (e.g.
  • stigmatized "problem areas") .
  • Functional Purpose: It serves to render community "calculable" for public administration
  • and governance .
  • Community Education
  • Empowerment Focus: Education is defined as "helping people to work together... to
  • grow in confidence and competence" to solve their own problems .
  • Participatory Methods: It involves "interactive planning exercises" and "surveys" that
  • enable the views of all sections of a community to be integrated .
  • Self-Determination:Unlike simple dissemination, education aims for "self-determination"
  • and "capacity-building".
  • Similarities and Differences
  • Similarities:Both are used as "tools for intervention" to manage community change and
  • regeneration. Both utilize research-based toolkits to assess local conditions.
  • Differences:Information dissemination is often more passive or regulatory, sometimes
  • being "done to" communities to manage conflict . Community education is more "active"
  • and "bottom-up," focusing on "giving the weak a voice" and enabling them to mobilize
  • collective power .
  • Both methods are important, but community education leads to more sustainable change.
questions.final_answer: Both methods are important, but community education leads to more sustainable change
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Discuss the relationship between social processes such as proverty, / unemployment,and marginalization and the need for human services
questions.solution_html:
• marginalization and the need for human services.
  • Social processes like poverty, unemployment, and marginalization negatively affect
  • individuals and communities.
  • Industrial Collapse: Economic restructuring has removed "organized production" from
  • many communities, leading to widespread unemployment and the loss of "industrial culture".
  • Concentrated Deprivation: These social processes create "wild zones" or estates that
  • become "dumping grounds" for "problem people," where community control over the streets
  • is lost .
  • Shift to Consumption:As production vanishes, the need for human services shifts toward
  • "collective consumption"—the provision of housing, health, and welfare by the state to
  • reproduce the workforce.
  • Human services are essential to address the negative effects of social problems and
  • promote well-being.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Examine how the concept of control differs between urban individualistic societies / and rural collectivistic communities
questions.solution_html:
• Examine how the concept of control differs between urban individualistic societies and
  • rural collectivistic communities.
  • Social control refers to mechanisms that regulate behavior in society.
  • Urban Individualism: Control is often formal and bureaucratic . Relationships are
  • "anonymous" and "transitory," leading individuals to cultivate "privacy" and rely on abstract
  • systems of information rather than personal trust .
  • Rural Collectivism: Control is deeply personal and rooted in "shared knowledge" . The
  • "community moral voice" exerts pressure to conform.
  • Surveillance: In rural settings, "everybody knows everybody else’s business," allowing for
  • continuous informal cementing of norms. In urban settings, control might involve "gated
  • communities" or "systems of surveillance" to regulate access.
  • Both systems have strengths and limitations; a balance between formal and informal control
  • is ideal.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
